blocks.x: You can see that little light and that tells where it's recording. Let's see, we're at 115... 115 West 145th Street. Yes, and my name is Dick Allen, this is my voice, and Danny Barker is the Chief Engineer.

When you're drumming? When I'm drumming, it's a habit I guess. Sometimes I'm very confident I got that stereo to my eyeball look. From your menstrual days? Yeah. I got them menstrual days, what do you call it? T-O-B-A.
Yeah, I know what that stands for.

So when I'm drumming and I think I'm drumming naturally, I ain't doing nothing, but the folks looking at me laughing. So I catch myself and try to straighten up. First thing you know, I'm still drumming, I get right back in that, that funny look again and people look at me, always looking at me, see. When I'm drumming, I call myself drumming natural. So I have them look around there and the people, aren't you going down the road? Laughing and just, I call it Black Down and Joe Giggle.

So I said to myself, well, I don't laugh at nobody but me. I said, you know, I must look mighty funny up there. So I asked, I said, what? I said, every time I look around, I said, what, what, what are you all laughing about?

He said, Fred, you make anybody laugh. So you got a certain way you look at a person, you make them laugh. So your eyes is going and, you know, stretching your eyes, your eyeballing, your head is going. So I had some pictures made, so I found out how I look after I had this picture made. T-O-B-A? T-O-B-A. That's what you call going around the world. Washington, Philadelphia, Baltimore.

And College Chauvinist was a volleyball circuit. The man was, was one time, was meant to be, to be an attraction. Yeah. Late artists call it, tough on black actors. Or something. Because they caught, they caught hell. Stranded when you went on to T-O-B-A if you didn't have a big name attraction, you were suddenly canceled or stranded.
Yeah. I know all about that. I've been stranded a man a day. And I missed a many of me or two. Oh, yeah.
What about New Orleans? You told me you made a trip down there. I went to New Orleans.

I'm, see, I can't remember the year. And I'm moving so fast. I got up to the sides. I went to New Orleans and, uh, William Benbow. He was another old producer. He had a bad age. Put your money in there. Yeah. He make the money, but he didn't want to pay the, pay the musician, the performance. But I, he don't owe me around about, he owed me around about three weeks. He would've owed me more, but I got a hip, a hip to myself. Always busting drum heads. I wouldn't bust no drum heads. I make turn I bust it. After the show, I take the drum head off and hide it. Tells Benbow I bust a drum head. How much a drum head cost? During that time it cost, but it cost a dollar and a half then. So he gave me a dollar and a half. I bust drum head every, every two weeks. That's three dollars. No, every week. That's three dollars. And I saved that money. And I, I guess I must've got around at least about fifty dollars out of him busting drum heads. I didn't, never did bust no round about two though, literally speaking. This guy kept upon getting some of my money. And I, I guess I must've got around at least about fifty dollars out of him busting drum heads. I didn't, never did bust no round about two though, literally speaking. This guy kept upon getting some of my money. And over in New Orleans, we played at their, what did their theater there DAnter?
The Lyric Theater?

The Lyric Theater. That's when I first met Professor Rogashow, the violin player. And I think they had about five or six pieces in the pit, probably more than that. I couldn't remember but two of them. Professor Rogashow was playing the violin and Red Happy. I called him Red. He's a great fly drummer, great show drummer. And we stayed there, stayed in the theater two weeks. And we went from the early, we went to Havana, Cuba. We stayed over there around, oh, about three months.
How do you like New Orleans as a city?
Well, I love it. I love it.
Did you go back around Basin Street after the show was over at night?

No. My whole hangout was after the show was over. I think you call it Pennell Street. What's the street that's called? Grand Point Street. Grand Point Street, yeah. I was mostly interested in good looking girls. Oh, yeah.
Yeah.

Did you see them in New Orleans? Oh, man, they got some beautiful girls here. Some real Creole girls. Are they very friendly and affectionate? Oh, yeah. You see them there from the darkest to the whitest. Pretty long hair, dreamy eyes. You don't want no stuff from me neither. And they're well built up? Oh, yeah, man. New shape. I mean, it was shape. Waist like a wasp and the backside like a horse.
Yeah.

So we went to, after you left New Orleans, we went to Havana Cuba. And we stayed down there about four months. We was following Gonzalo White. I think that was his name. And that's when I, first, first time I remember seeing rasters, little rasters, little drummer rasters. Great sensation drummer. I was kind of fly there during that time of set, but I wasn't fly as he was. He used to make a running spin slide on his stomach and hit the bass drum and cymbal right on the beat. The band would be playing. Any time he would be playing, he'd make a running thing the band was still playing and turn around and face the drum with two sticks and made a slide on his stomach. And on the end of the, on the end of the number, he would slide there just in time to hit that cymbal and bass drum. Vroom! He's a great little dancer too. He's a sensation drummer. He's one of the sensation drummers. I was getting $40 a week with Benbo. So when they come back, we played, we hit, we come out of the way by Key West Florida. We started playing all through Florida. How'd you like Cuba? Wonderful. Only thing about it, I learned to speak a few words in Spanish. I learned how to speak for, I asked for rice, yellow rice, or rice, yellow rice. Coffee with milk in it, coffee lector, as we have pronounced it. And beef, beef steak and potatoes, call it beef steak and papatritas. And when I see a good looking chick, I look at her, hey baby. She could understand what I was talking about, see. So I find out the way, what I would have said to somebody to talk and say, don't be talking about, hey baby. See, just take your hand and do this. She knew what you mean.
Like you're knocking on the door.
Yeah, she knew what you mean. So I picked up on one of them all like that. I said, hey baby.
She said, man, don't say no, hey baby, do this.

So I looked at the girl, got her eye, and I did this. And she come over to me. I said, you want to have a drink with me? She said, man, they don't know nobody speaking no, no. Speak Spanish. I said, all right, you be my intent, you speak funny. Tell her what I want to have a drink with. So I mean, let me come on back down, bed off in Florida.
But did you have it in the rum down there? Yeah. Did you have it in the Spanish cigars and cigarettes? Spanish cigarettes.

They're strong. Yeah, man. Yeah, they're strong. I tried with them, man, and things strangled me. I called myself, I never do very much smoking when I did smoke, when I started when I was a kid. And you went out to your mom to smoke that Spanish cigarette?
Yeah.
I used to smoke the Bull Durham tobacco.
But the Cuban cigarettes, did you go out your mind after you started seeing things when you smoked that cigarette?
Well, I tried, man, for the first time, the last time.
I think the guy, I think he'd give it to me.
He didn't say it to me, he'd give it to me. He'd give it to me. During that time, I would say it was 10 cents a piece or 15 or 25 cents a piece, something like that.
It slipped you the wrong kind of cigarette, though.

Yeah. So I didn't know what it was. I just lit it and tried to inhale like I did a, like I do a cigarette. Tell me you ain't supposed to smoke them like that. I don't know about them today. I was like, oh, I'm a little bit of a cigarette. And then, uh, so I took a big inhale on it. I started coughing and barking and sneezing going on. I said, man, I woke up the fingers just yet. I said, man, that's a Spanish cigarette, a Spanish cigarette. And about 15, 20 minutes, man, I was, I was, my eyes was bucked and I was trembling all over. I was talking out in the head and acting all foolish. I was, I was talking, I was, I was talking loud. I don't know what I was saying. Using all kinds of Spanish words. Yeah, and I was trying to use them big words and Spanish words. So when I got to Barcelona, Spain, I learned how to speak a little bit more. A little more, uh, Spanish.
Did you see a bullfight over there?
Yeah. The people over there in, in Barcelona, Spain, were very friendly. In fact, they speak a lot of English over there, too.
So, back to Red Happy. What style of drumming would he use? Would he beat 4-4 or 2-4? Or both or what? He beat both. They used both, huh?

Both. And his show, show drumming, some drumming, type of the, uh, in some numbers called for, what they call, beat two. I mean, two beat. That mean the foundation, to hold a band together. Mm-hmm. In some numbers he beat four. But he was good on both of them. Mm-hmm. He was what you call a foundation drummer. And a fly drummer, too.
But what does a fly drummer do like him?

Well, a fly drummer takes solo, take a lot of tricks. Drums, solos, and cleave control. Throw the sticks up in the air. And Red Happy did all that? Yeah, throw the sticks up in the air and kept them all behind them. He was using around like four or five sticks. That's the apocondy line, he used four sticks. I use four sticks now. All at once? Yeah. What do you do? Well, I have, I have two on my arm. Mm-hmm.
And two on my hand. See?

If I have some sticks, I'll demonstrate it to you. Yeah, well, is it like juggling? Is that what it is? Something like juggling, but you're moving with rhythm. Mm-hmm. I mean, you can't, you know, I can't speak for that. You switch the sticks around. Yeah. Well, you take a stick from here and put it in your mouth. Yeah. You take a stick from here and put it in your mouth. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.

Yeah. You take a stick from here and put it in your mouth. Mm-hmm. See? You take it from here and put it in this arm. You're moving all the time. There's a picture. Yeah. Right in the rhythm. I used to use eight sticks. No, nine sticks I used to use. But I have to be sitting in a straight chair to use nine sticks. I put one on each side here I'm sitting on. I put a stick stand up if I can get to them. I have one between the legs and two on the bass drum. Mm-hmm. And still have me stick some arms. Oh, yeah. And I'm drumming still. I've got to use a space to put the other stick, the third stick all the time. It seems very complicated, but I used to use, I could use nine sticks better than I could four. I could balance myself better like that. But I can't sit on a drum stool. I have to sit on a regular square chair to do that. And I, since I've been, since I got a little bit ageable, I can't drum sitting down low. I have to sit up high, take that weight off my, to care for my leg. You sit down low, drum, any drummer sit down low. You can't, they can't keep them four beats up all the way through. They get tired in there, in the end step or even in the catheter's leg. You've got to sit up high and have some support up in here. You've got to stiffen the muscles in there for your four.
Yeah. Oh, when were you with Joe Oliver? That's another thing I wanted to say.
Well, I joined Joe Oliver 1929, right here in New York. Of course, that wasn't the first job I had. The first job I had was, Wafwa was a Wilma Sweatman.
Oh, yeah.

I rehearsed with him about a couple of months, especially for this job. He used, he used to use three clarinets one time. Well, there wasn't clarinets. One of them I think was, what you call that thing, O-Bo, not O-Bo, but a thing like a, uh, a- Clarinet, a Zoom? Yeah, a Zoom, clarinet. Two clarinets, a Zoom. Zoom in the middle of the mouth, two clarinets on the side. First job I had here, I think that was, a little before, around about the first, first of 29, I played with him at the Lockhead Theater. Yeah, New York. It wasn't but three of us. I was a little bit of a play.
Who was the other fellow?

Uh, the girl's name, the girl named Piano Fash. Used to tell what New York was, the old lady New York was the violin player. I can't remember the name. Jerry Smith? Jerry Smith, yeah, she was on the piano. And, uh, I was playing the clarinet and I was on drums. They're trio trio. He used to play a number like the roses reading them, you know. And, uh, anyway. So we rehearsed this act. About a couple of months we got it together. And, uh, we was booked in this, uh, July 5th theater. For a week. But we stayed two weeks. every stage two weeks. And I think the scale was there during that time was $55. Well, the man didn't want to pay, I have no two drummers. So he asked me, could I play the show? Yeah, I play the show. He said, well, I'll tell you what to do. He said, if you play the show, you'll make your salary $90 altogether. That was big money for me then, you know. I've never got that kind of money before. That's how I was getting around $40. So, play the show. And after I finished those two weeks, the first week, rather, the union man was there. I come in on a transfer. What you call a transfer, you know, like I belong to some other unions, don't belong to this union. But the first, the first week I worked, I don't know the man that's lacking me, I haven't taken a chance or something, what it was. Anyway, he taken, he taken half of my money to join the union. I think it was $54 to join the union. So, I think it was $35. He knew we were going to get another week, so he was going to take the rest of it, you know. So, anyway, I had to pay $54 to join the union. Then I took a visa for a while around here. King Oliver. Then, I seen this boy, Dave Nelson. Dave Nelson was King Oliver's right-hand band during that time. Dave Nelson used to do all the arranging, like music, for the band. So, he asked me, say, Boy, I said, I'd like you working very much. I see you still there, I said. I said, you want to join, join King Oliver? I said, I'm the leader of the band. I said, who? King Oliver. You ever heard of King Oliver? I said, yeah, I heard of King Oliver. You want to join? I said, yeah. How's the money? I said, we're able to talk about it, see whether he's lacking that. I said, we're going to have rehearsal tomorrow. So, he said, you come to rehearsal, see. Bring the drums. Bring the drums, yeah. Bring the drums, yeah. Bring the drums, I'm not allowed. So, I brought my drums, set them up. During that time, it had, it had 12-piece band. And, and I went too sharp on my reading. I could spell kind of slow. The most important thing, I was worried about, playing the introductions, first and second ending, and the quarter as the main thing.
Can you explain that first and second ending to me?

Well, the first course, you repeat the first course. You got your little dots up there, they tell you to repeat. You play the first course twice, if you want to. And you jump to the second ending, something like a modulation, something like a modulation, like, but the rhythm is still going. Then you go in, the second ending, the course, you're going into the last course. Now, you can play that second ending twice, if you want to. Or you can play it once. But the introduction is tricky. Second ending is tricky. Especially the quarter is the last course, the end of the course. That's very tricky. You got to know what you're doing. You might have two bars out. You might have three bars out. I have four. But when you, you got to count. When the drummer is supposed to be, lay out four bars, the other band is playing. But you're laying out four bars. But some of the other, the rhythm is doing something else. But you got to know when they come in, you got to be, you got to count. Otherwise, you got to count about two, three bars while you're playing ahead. You know, like you're playing here. You got to count two bars ahead. Read ahead all the time. Read ahead all the time. Two bars ahead all the time. So I like to read enough to play shows.
So I, I'd like to read when King Howard, what he was like with you.

Oh, he come to like me very much. We were like to show, we were like to got the band together. We were talking about, say about, about two weeks, we were like to band. Got him put a fair shake. And the first thing he had a recording date, he recorded in with, uh, for Victor, Bramjit, and Columbia. And, uh, he was calling for about five different companies. So I didn't know nothing about, you know, that kind of money. He was only paying, I think it was $30 a session.
Record date.

Yeah, record date. Full size. Four records or something. $30. So I, I wanted my money so bad. I need the money so bad, sir. It always take about three weeks before you get your money. So King Howard used to buy me out. So he'd give me $20, $25 right then, so I'd get a record and put it out of my own pocket and pay me right then. I didn't have to wait. Left the fellas of the band, he'd wait to, wait to three or four weeks before the record come out, I mean, before, you know, for the issue of the record. So I'd get my money and then spend it. Anyway, you made your records.
Remember the films?
Yeah, some of them was, uh, Mule Face and Boogie Woogie. Edna. Edna, Scruggled Buggy, Shake It and Break It. I got that. Yeah.
When you smiling, how was Joe playing?

Well, he, he was playing fair. He'd always could play good, but his, he had that, uh, his teeth wouldn't let him play too high. See, his teeth, he had that, what you call it, a pair of red. A pair of red. On his teeth. And when he, during the time he was recording, he had different trumpet players. He had guys like, uh, Ward Pinky and Louis Medcalf and Henry Red Allen. All them boys. Used to help him out. Or we used to make, uh, sometimes we'd make about two or three playbacks. And the only reason why we'd make this kind of all the minute playbacks, because Joe would crack up. He couldn't, he hit the, uh, he tried to hit a note, but his lip wouldn't, wouldn't let him. So they'd cut it off, keep on, make them over and over. So they got, uh, had their, uh, Red Allen on some of them. Louis Medcalf and Dave Nelson.
Where was Dave from? New Orleans.
He's from New Orleans. Yeah. New Orleans was there. Left New Orleans earlier, you know, settled in Chicago, I suppose.

He was, uh, he was a trumpet player and could play piano too. And arranged. And arranged, great arranger. In fact, he did all the arranging mostly for, uh, Joe Oliver after, after, after Joe and Louis broke up.
Did you ever hear that record, Stingery Blues, that Joe Oliver made? I made that thing. Oh, you made it?
Yeah. Yeah. I forgot to call that. Stingery Blues.
I think you can hear Dave Nelson on it pretty good, I believe that's him. I'm not sure. Could be.

Yeah, I played it for, uh, Paul Barber one time. But during that time, when he recorded, you kept your bass drum padded. Mm-hmm. You put quilts and all, everything in front of the bass. You didn't want to hear no bass drum. All you want to hear that snare drum, snare so down low, like a tom-tom effect, not quite a tom-tom effect. Mm-hmm. And when you hit the cymbal, you don't hit it with the sticks. You use a soft mallet. Mm-hmm. You hit the cymbal and choke it. Cut it off.
You make the needle jump on the record some days.

Yeah. You couldn't use the sticks and pound on them like it, you know. You couldn't. Where would they make you sit, a drummer? Would he be in close to the microphone or far from it or what? Close to the mic. Pretty close. Yeah, pretty close. I had a mic hanging right over.
But they'd have old pillars and quilts and things. In the front of the drum, keep it in the middle. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. recording through those long horns. What you call them things? Yeah, the microphone. Didn't have it set up that they got now, you know, the different things.
Well, how would that change your style to record? What would you do different?
You wouldn't stand playing somewhat softer on it.
You wouldn't change your style. You just play soft and use your mallets.
Could you use your wood blocks, for example? Oh yeah, your wood blocks.

You could use wood blocks. Yeah, your wood blocks. And your car bell. You work with Jelly too? Well, I've done something with Jelly, Jelly at old Martin. How about? Oh, about two months. He had his, had about four or five automobiles, Cadillacs. Lincoln. Lincoln, yeah. So he diamonds? Yeah. He's playing all through Redding, Pennsylvania, and Philadelphia. Next time. Yeah. That's great. Yeah. He's playing them one night stands, you know. Sometimes the cars, one or two of the cars would break down. One or two of the jobs we didn't make. Car broke down. Some of the fellas got there, waiting on us, on the drummer. The car was in. Broke down. The drummer wasn't there. So when we did get there, we supposed to start at 9 o'clock. From 9 to 1. When we did get there, we got there at 11 o'clock. Everybody done demand the money back. We didn't get paid for that job. Jelly at old was a good fellow. He was a great piano player. If he hadn't had a, had a bus, he started those cars. A little up-to-date bus, he started those cars. But his car was kind of old, I don't know how he was. 38, 39. Yeah, probably.
Jelly roll, did a lot of talking, lecturing. Yeah.

Love the talking. Yeah, he sat on the pianos to them, crossed his legs and tell them. Different things about music, how he first started. He hit a chord, boom, boom, boom. And he'd tell you what it's all about, you know.
He'd do that in person when you saw him, huh?

Yeah. I mean, sometime before the band starts, the band would sit up on the wall set up. He said, ladies and gentlemen, my name is General Martin. I'm surrounded by my band. He called all names then, because that was a long time ago, you know. He called a boy's name. He said, we're going to beat out a little rhythm here to call one of my tunes, call it, uh... What's that tune?
Shoe Shine's Rag. Yeah.

Shoe Shine's Rag. Yeah. Shoe Postal. Yeah. The 12s. Yeah. Then he'd hit one or two chords, demonstrate, tell them that's where you're going. That's when the band was going to sound when he starts. He'd hit a chord and explain to the people what that chord meant, what he was going to do, you know. When he start off, he start the band off, he never beat no, uh... Never beat the temple off modern like, uh, like the fellas do here in New York. He never beat no four beats. He stomped his foot down on, on the naked floor. Something like this. That's all. The band right with it. He never, never do that. He may hit one for tripletion. That's not what to get the band together. Mm-hmm. The tension. He might do it twice. There. That's the temple right there.

They still do that, down in New Orleans, I've seen this. Did you ever hear about Joe Oliver? One time he wanted the band to go out. That's happening to all this. Eddie Dawson told me about this. And they never would pay any attention. He'd stomp his foot, and that meant to go out, you know? Finish his foot. So, one day he had a brick in his trumpet case. So instead of stomping his foot, Frank threw it down on the floor. One beat means, one beat means that, after you finish the number, one beat means that you're going out, you're finishing the coast. Yeah. Well, he didn't use that same system, and he used a brick to make sure that he made.
Joe Oliver used to, well, he didn't do it. Well, he meant it, he meant business, but he called it rehearsal.
He mean one of everybody there. Oh, yeah.
Well, he didn't exactly mean what he was doing, but that's his way. When he come called rehearsal, he bring his gun with him, you know? Great gun about that long.
Eight, nine inches long.

Yeah. And so he got this big table up there in front of the bandstand, where he sit. Sometime he rehearsed the band, but Dave Nelson rehearsed the band. So Joe Oliver, when he come in, he's walking very slow, look everybody over, with that Google eye, and pull out this long pistol, put it on up that side of the music, and look around. Is everybody here?
Dave Yord here. Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .
Okay, it's ready, it's going. Now, we'll start. My name is Fred Moore. King Oliver, former drummer.
